description: God's nature, goodness, and the problem of evil and human suffering.
content_html:
What Is God Like?

One of the biggest questions in philosophy and religion is: what is God actually like? Religious traditions answer this question in rich and varied ways. Most Christians understand God through three key qualities: God is omnipotent, knowing everything past, present and future (omniscient), and perfectly good. These qualities are called the “divine attributes.” For many believers, understanding God’s nature is essential — it shapes how they pray, how they act, and how they make sense of suffering.

Christians believe God is deeply personal: a being who created the universe not out of necessity but out of love, and who continues to be involved in the lives of people. The letter of 1 John 4:8 makes this claim directly: “God is love.” This short statement carries enormous weight. It suggests that love is not just something God does — it is what God fundamentally is. This framing shapes how Christians respond to suffering and evil.

Key Fact

The three core divine attributes are omnipotence (all-powerful), omniscience (all-knowing) and omnibenevolence (all-loving or all-good). Together they form the classical theistic view of God and provide the basis for the problem of evil.

God’s Relationship With the World

Believers also debate how God relates to the world he created. A transcendent God is utterly beyond the universe — distant, wholly other, not directly involved in day-to-day events. By contrast, an immanent God is close and personally active, felt in everyday life. Most mainstream Christian traditions hold both: God is transcendent in greatness and yet immanent through the Holy Spirit, prayer, and the life of Jesus Christ.

The parable of the Prodigal Son in Luke 15:11–32 captures this sense of an immanent, personally involved God. The father in the story runs to meet his returning son — a picture of God actively pursuing a relationship with humanity rather than remaining remote. For believers, this parable shows that God’s relationship with the world is not passive but active and loving.

God as Good: What Does Goodness Mean?

Religious believers argue that God is the source and standard of all goodness. Genesis 1:31 records that after God finished creation, “God saw all that he had made, and it was very good.” This suggests that goodness is built into the fabric of creation. God does not merely follow a moral code that exists independently — God is the moral order. When believers say God is good, they mean his actions, character and purposes are never destructive or selfish.

However, believers disagree about what divine goodness means in practice. Some argue that God’s goodness is the same as human moral goodness, only perfect. Others say God’s goodness is so far beyond human understanding that we can only speak of it by analogy. The medieval thinker Thomas Aquinas argued we use language about God “analogically” — terms like “good” apply to God in a related but not identical way to how they apply to people.

Many Christians believe God’s goodness is expressed through his benevolence — his care and mercy towards all humanity. They point to passages like Psalm 23 (“The Lord is my shepherd”) and the Sermon on the Mount, where Jesus calls his followers to reflect God’s goodness through love, compassion and justice.

Some denominations, particularly within the Reformed tradition, emphasise God’s justice alongside his love — arguing that goodness also means God cannot ignore wrongdoing. Evangelical Christians often stress that God’s goodness is shown supremely in the sacrifice of Jesus Christ, who took on human sin so that people could be forgiven and restored to relationship with God.

The Problem of Evil and Suffering

The most challenging objection to belief in God is the problem of evil. The argument runs like this: if God is omnipotent, he could prevent suffering. If he is omnibenevolent, he would want to prevent it. Yet suffering clearly exists. So either God is not all-powerful, or not all-good — or does not exist at all. This is what philosophers call the “logical problem of evil.”

Suffering takes two forms. Moral evil arises from human choices — such as violence, theft or oppression. Natural evil arises from the natural world — earthquakes, cancer, floods. Non-believers often argue that natural evil is especially difficult to explain, since it cannot be blamed on human free will.

Key Fact

Moral evil and natural evil together form the “problem of evil.” The dilemma is ancient: it was expressed in Psalm 22:1 when the psalmist cries, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” — and in the Book of Job, where a righteous man suffers without apparent cause.

Religious Responses to Suffering

Religious believers have developed a range of responses to this challenge. One of the most important is the “free will defence.” God gave humans free will — the genuine ability to choose good or evil. Without this freedom, human beings would be moral robots, incapable of love or virtue. Moral evil is therefore a consequence of human freedom, not evidence against God’s goodness.

A second response concerns the purpose of suffering. The prophet Jeremiah, speaking on God’s behalf in Jeremiah 5:19, frames suffering as a consequence of turning away from God — a call to return. This does not mean God causes every individual suffering as punishment, but that suffering can prompt repentance, growth and a deeper relationship with God.

Many believers also point to the example of Jesus Christ, who suffered on the cross. Far from being absent from suffering, in the Christian tradition God entered into it. This is called the “theology of the cross” or divine solidarity. For many Christians, the resurrection then shows that suffering does not have the final word.

Atheists and agnostics argue that the existence of widespread, apparently pointless suffering is strong evidence against an all-powerful, all-good God. The philosopher J.L. Mackie argued that the co-existence of God and evil is a logical contradiction — a truly omnipotent God could create free beings who always freely chose good.

Humanists respond to suffering by emphasising human responsibility: rather than praying for divine intervention, the moral response is human action — working to reduce poverty, disease and injustice. Many non-believers also argue that natural disasters show a universe that is indifferent to human welfare, not one designed by a loving creator. In a 15-mark “Discuss” response, presenting these views fairly alongside religious responses demonstrates the evaluative thinking examiners reward.

The Islamic tradition also engages with this question. Muslims affirm that Allah is Ar-Rahman (the Most Gracious) and Ar-Rahim (the Most Merciful), and that trials and suffering are a test of faith and a means of spiritual purification, not evidence of divine absence. This perspective reflects the multi-faith nature of the theme as examined on this paper.
exam_tip_html: On the 15-mark “Discuss” question, examiners want a genuine dialogue between viewpoints. For a topic like God’s goodness and the problem of evil, a strong response will present the logical problem of evil clearly, give at least two religious responses (such as the free will defence and the theology of the cross), and then weigh them honestly — acknowledging where they do and do not satisfy the objection — before reaching a justified conclusion. A common student error is to list responses without evaluating them. Remember: the 15-mark question is AO2-weighted, meaning evaluation earns more marks than description. Also, SPaG is assessed here — spell key terms correctly: “omnibenevolence,” “omnipotent,” “transcendent,” “immanent.” For 6-mark “Explain” questions, always anchor your answer in a source of wisdom: a scripture verse or named theological position.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • God is understood in most Christian and Islamic traditions as omnipotent, omniscient and omnibenevolent; “God is love” (1 John 4:8) is a central expression of divine goodness, while the Parable of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11–32) illustrates God as personally involved and forgiving.
  • The problem of evil asks: if God is all-powerful and all-good, why does suffering exist? Two types of suffering matter: moral evil (caused by human choices) and natural evil (caused by natural events). Psalm 22:1 and the Book of Job reflect this ancient struggle.
  • Religious responses include the free will defence, the idea that suffering prompts spiritual growth, and the “theology of the cross” (divine solidarity in suffering). Non-religious thinkers argue that widespread pointless suffering counts as evidence against God’s existence — a view to engage critically, not ignore.

practice_questions.text: State one Christian teaching about the nature of God.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of the following: God is omnipotent / omniscient / omnibenevolent / loving / transcendent / immanent / personal. Accept any accurate statement of a divine attribute supported by the tradition. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what religious believers mean when they say God is omnibenevolent.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks: omnibenevolent means all-good or all-loving (1 mark); this means God acts with perfect goodness and love towards all people at all times, as expressed in 1 John 4:8 (‘God is love’) (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline two religious responses to the problem of evil and suffering.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for each of two responses identified (e.g. the free will defence; suffering as a spiritual test/means of growth; divine solidarity/theology of the cross), plus 1 mark for developing one of them (e.g. without free will humans could not genuinely love God). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which a believer might respond to the challenge that God cannot be good if evil and suffering exist.
Refer to sources of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 6 marks (3 per response): 1 mark for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a relevant source. Example responses: (1) Free will defence — God gave humans genuine free will so that love and virtue are possible; moral evil is a consequence of human freedom, not of God’s failure; Genesis 1:31 shows God’s creation was originally ‘very good’. (2) Theology of the cross — God entered into human suffering through Jesus Christ; the crucifixion shows divine solidarity; the resurrection promises suffering does not have the final word. (3) Suffering as a call to return — Jeremiah 5:19 frames suffering as a consequence of turning from God and an invitation to renewed relationship. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The existence of evil and suffering proves that God does not exist.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: The logical problem of evil (Mackie) argues that an omnipotent, omnibenevolent God and evil cannot co-exist; if God could prevent suffering and does not, he is either not all-powerful or not all-good. Natural evil — earthquakes, disease — cannot be blamed on human choices, making the free will defence insufficient for this category of suffering. Humanists point out that a universe of random, pointless suffering fits an atheistic worldview far better than a theistic one.

Arguments against: The free will defence: genuine love requires genuine freedom; moral evil is the result of human choices, not divine cruelty. The theology of the cross: God does not stand apart from suffering but entered into it through Jesus Christ (Psalm 22:1 is quoted by Jesus on the cross, showing God understands abandonment). Soul-making response: suffering enables moral and spiritual development; a world of no challenge would prevent the growth of virtues such as courage and compassion. Islamic perspective: trials test and purify faith; Allah’s mercy (‘Ar-Rahim’) encompasses even suffering.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources or thinkers; clear weighing of arguments (e.g. noting which type of evil each response handles best); justified personal conclusion.
Secure: Both sides presented with some development and at least one source; conclusion present.
Developing: Both sides attempted but unevenly developed; limited use of sources; conclusion may be weak.
Emerging: One-sided or very brief; few or no sources; little to no conclusion. [15 marks; SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Explain two different ways in which Christians understand God's relationship with the world.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 6 marks (3 per way): 1 mark for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with source. Example responses: (1) God as transcendent — utterly beyond and outside the universe, not directly involved in earthly events; some denominations, particularly in the Reformed tradition, emphasise God’s sovereignty and otherness. (2) God as immanent — personally present and active in the world; the Parable of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11–32) depicts a God who runs to meet returning sinners; the Holy Spirit is understood as God’s continuing presence in believers’ lives. [6 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which term means 'all-good' or 'all-loving' when describing God's nature?
Which type of evil is caused by natural events such as earthquakes and disease, rather than by human beings?
The phrase 'God is _____' from 1 John 4:8 is one of the most direct biblical statements about God's nature.
The _____ defence argues that God allows moral evil because he gave humans the genuine ability to choose between good and evil.
Match each term to its correct meaning:
right: God existing beyond and outside the physical universe
God present and active within the physical world
God being perfectly and completely good or loving

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'omnibenevolent' mean when applied to God?
flashcard_questions.a: All-good or all-loving; God's character and actions are perfectly and completely good.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the 'problem of evil' in philosophy of religion?
flashcard_questions.a: If God is all-powerful and all-good, why does evil and suffering exist?

flashcard_questions.q: What does 1 John 4:8 say about the nature of God?
flashcard_questions.a: 'God is love' — love is not merely what God does but what God fundamentally is.

flashcard_questions.q: What parable in Luke 15 illustrates God as immanent and personally involved?
flashcard_questions.a: The Parable of the Prodigal Son, where the father runs to meet his returning son.
Suffering caused by human choices, such as violence, cruelty or injustice.
Suffering caused by natural events such as earthquakes, disease or floods.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Genesis 1:31 say, and why does it matter for the problem of evil?
flashcard_questions.a: God saw all he had made was 'very good' — suggesting evil entered creation later through the Fall.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the 'free will defence' against the problem of evil?
flashcard_questions.a: God gave humans genuine free will; moral evil results from human choices, not divine failure.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'transcendent' mean as a divine attribute?
flashcard_questions.a: God exists beyond and entirely outside the physical universe.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'immanent' mean as a divine attribute?
flashcard_questions.a: God is present within and active throughout the physical world and human experience.

flashcard_questions.q: Which psalm opens with 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' — reflecting the problem of suffering?
What is 'divine solidarity' in the Christian response to suffering?
flashcard_questions.a: The idea that God entered into human suffering through the crucifixion of Jesus Christ.

glossary_terms.definition: The supreme being worshipped in monotheistic religions, understood to be eternal, all-powerful, all-knowing and perfectly good.
All-powerful; able to do anything that is logically possible.
The quality of being perfectly and completely good in character and action, attributed to God.
A view of God as existing beyond and entirely outside the physical universe.
A view of God as present within and throughout the physical world and in human experience.
Suffering caused by the actions of human beings, such as war, crime or cruelty.
Suffering caused by natural events rather than by human beings, such as earthquakes, disease or floods.
A quality of God expressed through mercy, compassion and unconditional love towards all people.
The idea that God enters into and shares in human suffering rather than remaining distant from it, seen especially in the crucifixion of Jesus.
